topic: Diagnosing biased samples and mismatched probability denominators
subtitle: Find and fix the mistake: wrong totals under a probability, samples that were never random, and counts that changed after a draw

traps.desc: used the number of blue counters as the denominator instead of the total number of counters

problems.desc: Student must name the error, not just correct it: the denominator of a probability is the total number of equally likely outcomes, and 7 is the number of blue counters rather than the total of 12. Full credit needs the words total number of counters, or an equivalent statement that the denominator must count every counter in the bag.

Student must say the sample is not random and explain the direction of the problem: only students who stayed late in the library were asked, and those students are more likely to be doing a lot of homework, so the estimate of 95 minutes is probably too high for the school as a whole. Full credit needs the reason the group was unusual, not just the word biased.

traps.desc: kept the counts from before the sweet was eaten

problems.desc: Student must name the error: eating a green sweet changes both counts, so the top drops from 4 to 3 and the bottom from 10 to 9. Full credit needs both changes, or an equivalent statement that the totals must be recounted after the sweet is removed; noticing only that the total changed is half the answer.

traps.desc: gave the probability of landing on red instead of the probability of not landing on red

problems.desc: Student must name the error: the favourable outcomes for not red are the 8 sections that are blue or green, so the top of the fraction is wrong even though the bottom of 12 is right. Full credit needs the correct favourable count identified, or the equivalent statement that the answer is one minus the probability of red.

Student must explain that everyone in the sample was already at the cinema, so the sample cannot represent the town: people who never go to the cinema had no chance of being asked. Full credit needs that the group was selected by the very behaviour being measured, and a statement that the estimate is therefore too high.
problems.slot: (b) why the estimate cannot be trusted

traps.desc: used the counts from before the card was removed

problems.desc: Student must name the error: the card that was removed is itself odd, so both counts fall -- the odd cards from 10 to 9 and the pack from 20 to 19. Full credit needs the point that the removed card was one of the favourable ones, so it comes off the top as well as the bottom.

traps.desc: used the 18 instrument players as the denominator instead of the whole class

problems.desc: Student must name the error: the question picks a student from the whole class, so the denominator is 30, not the 18 who play an instrument. Full credit needs the observation that the denominator has to match the group the choice is made from; a fraction out of 18 answers a different question, namely the chance that a player also sings.

Student must identify the self-selection problem: the 40 who replied chose themselves, and members keen on the trip are the ones most likely to answer, so the fraction saying yes is higher among repliers than among all 250 members and the estimate is too high. Full credit needs the self-selection point plus the direction of the error.
problems.slot: (b) what is wrong with the sample

problems.desc: Any method earns credit that gives every one of the 250 members the same chance of being counted: number all the members and draw a sample at random, then follow up until those chosen have answered, rather than accepting whoever replies. A response that simply says to email everyone again does not, because it repeats the same self-selection.
